questions.stem: Why is English word order (SVO) so rigid, according to the lecture?
options: Nouns basically have only two forms (singular and plural)
Word position must do the work of conveying meaning
English has very little inflection
Word endings indicate grammatical relationships, as in Russian
questions.explanation: In Russian, Finnish or Hungarian, inflections show relationships, so order is freer; English relies on position.

options: "Captopril" answers "Who or what controls?" and is the subject
"hypertension" is the subject because it is a disease
"hypertension" is the object
"controls" is the verb
questions.explanation: Find the verb, ask "who/what + verb?" for the subject, then "subject + verb + what?" for the object.

questions.stem: "The surgeon examined the patient" vs "The patient examined the surgeon" shows that:
options: In clinical documentation this precision can affect patient safety
Word order determines meaning in English
The same words can convey completely different meanings
Word order does not matter if the vocabulary is correct
questions.explanation: Meaning in English is determined primarily by word order.

options: Does the patient have diabetes?
When the symptoms did start?
Does the patient has diabetes?
When did the symptoms start?
questions.explanation: After does, use the base form (have). In wh- questions the auxiliary comes after the wh-word and before the subject.

questions.stem: The structure of a wh- question is:
options: Wh-word + Auxiliary + Subject + Main verb
Wh-word + Subject + Auxiliary + Main verb
Auxiliary + Wh-word + Subject + Main verb
Subject + Wh-word + Main verb
questions.explanation: e.g. "How long has she been in pain?". Yes/no questions are Aux + S + V.

questions.stem: In a medical consultation, according to the lecture:
options: Yes/no questions are useful for confirming information
"When did the pain begin?" is a yes/no question
Wh- questions are essential for open-ended history-taking
"Do you have a history of hypertension?" is a yes/no question
questions.explanation: "When did the pain begin?" is a wh- question.

options: The patient does not have a fever.
The infection cannot be ruled out.
The patient not has a fever.
She has not experienced any side effects.
questions.explanation: Negative structure: Subject + Auxiliary + not + Main verb.

questions.stem: About negative findings in clinical documentation:
options: They help establish differential diagnoses
They should be left out of notes to save space
They are as clinically significant as positive findings
"No evidence of fracture was found on X-ray" is an example
questions.explanation: Negation is crucial for ruling out diagnoses and documenting negative findings.

options: "Treatment began immediately." — interrogative
"Has she experienced any side effects?" — interrogative
"The infection cannot be ruled out." — negative
"The diagnosis was confirmed by the blood test." — declarative
questions.explanation: "Treatment began immediately" is a declarative sentence with an intransitive verb.

questions.stem: Match the sentence to its pattern:
options: "Blood flows." — Pattern 1 (S + intransitive V)
"Gallbladder stores bile." — Pattern 3 (S + transitive V + DO)
"The patient remains stable." — Pattern 7 (S + linking V + Adj)
"The liver is an essential organ." — Pattern 7 (S + linking V + Adj)
questions.explanation: "The liver is an essential organ" has a noun complement: Pattern 6.

questions.stem: "The hospital named Dr. Funes the best surgeon." This sentence:
options: Is Pattern 5
Uses a linking verb
Has a direct object followed by an object complement
Has two nouns that refer to the same person
questions.explanation: Pattern 5: S + V + N (DO) + N (OC) — Dr. Funes and "the best surgeon" are the same person. "Named" is not a linking verb.

questions.stem: Which sentences contain a linking verb followed by a subject complement?
options: The surgeon performed the operation.
The patient became a diabetic.
The test results are inconclusive.
The diagnosis is pneumonia.
questions.explanation: became/are/is are linking verbs (patterns 6 and 7). "performed the operation" is transitive + direct object (pattern 3).

questions.stem: Which pattern does "The heart lies in the thoracic cavity" follow?
options: S + linking V + noun (Pattern 6)
S + intransitive V + adverbial (Pattern 2)
S + V + DO + IO (Pattern 4)
S + transitive V + DO (Pattern 3)
questions.explanation: Pattern 2 adds information about how, when or where; "lies" takes no object.

questions.stem: Which are recommendations or corrections given in the lecture?
options: Keep the subject and verb close together
Place long phrases between the subject and the verb for emphasis
"After waiting for three hours, the patient was finally seen" is preferred
Prefer the active voice for clarity: "The doctor examined the patient."
questions.explanation: Overuse of the passive and separating subject and verb are listed as common errors.

questions.stem: Rearrange "with / presents / pain / the / chest / patient". The correct sentence is:
options: Presents the patient with chest pain.
The patient presents with chest pain.
The chest presents with patient pain.
The patient with chest pain presents.
questions.explanation: Subject (the patient) + verb (presents) + prepositional phrase (with chest pain).

questions.stem: Which are the three core sentence types this lecture presents for clinical communication?
options: Interrogative
Negative
Exclamatory
Declarative
questions.explanation: Declarative (stating facts), interrogative (history-taking questions), negative (excluding symptoms or findings).
